# fctl

> fctl is an open source software factory for Claude Code. People, scripts and other agents describe work; fctl runs Claude Code agents on it in isolated Linux sandboxes on machines the team owns, around the clock, on the Claude subscriptions of the people who start them, never on API billing. Each piece of work is a session: one Claude conversation in its own sandbox, on its own git branch, usually ending in a pull request that the agent comes back to for review comments, failed checks and conflicts. Everything is reachable from the web app, the `fctl` CLI (every command takes `--json`) and an HTTP API.

This file is for agents and the people who set them up: what fctl is, the words it uses, how to drive it safely from a terminal or another program, recipes for common flows, what to avoid, and where the details are. It is served at https://fctl.sh/llms.txt, at `/llms.txt` of every fctl instance (such as https://app.fctl.sh/llms.txt), and kept in the repository as `docs/llms.txt`. Every doc page is also served as Markdown (`https://fctl.sh/docs/<page>.md`), and https://fctl.sh/llms-full.txt is this file followed by all the docs in one file. For flags, `fctl <command> --help` has the final word.

fctl is open source under the MIT license: https://github.com/hyperstructure/fctl. https://app.fctl.sh is a managed control plane that hyperstructure runs (by invitation or early access); anyone can host all of fctl themselves, on Cloudflare or in one container ([Self-hosting](https://fctl.sh/docs/self-hosting.md)).

## What fctl gives you

- **Unattended agents in sandboxes.** Each session runs Claude Code with permission prompts off inside its own Linux VM or container on a runner (a Mac with Apple's `container`, Lima, Docker, or a Linux machine's Firecracker microVMs). The agent clones the project's repository, works on a branch named `fctl/<number>-<title>`, commits, and fctl pushes after every turn; it opens a pull request when the task is done, unless the project turns that off.
- **Live, steerable work.** Every event is journaled and streamed: follow a session in the web app, in a terminal (`fctl attach`), or in the Claude apps (Remote Control, with a full Claude login). Message the agent at any time (with files), interrupt its turn, stop it, resume it later in the same sandbox and conversation.
- **Work that starts itself.** Schedules (cron, once at a time, each time something happens on GitHub such as an issue opened, a pull request merged or checks failing on main, or only when asked), Linear (assign or mention fctl on an issue), GitHub Actions and any tool that can make an HTTP request with an access token.
- **Webhooks to your tools.** A workspace's or a project's webhooks post what happens as it happens, signed as Standard Webhooks sign them: a session started, finished a turn, asked something, has its pull requests ready for review (checks passed, no review agent at work), was brought back by a follow-up, paused, stopped or failed; an agent's pull request opened, merged or closed; a review queued, started, posted (with its findings), failed or cancelled; a schedule's run that started nothing. An address answers fctl's challenge (`url_verification`) before a webhook posts there, and a webhook posts only while whoever chose its address (added it, pointed it there or turned it on) still manages it: fctl turns it off once they left or lost the role. Failed requests go again 7 times over about 21 hours, and each webhook's log keeps what went out, the newest 1,000 of the last 30 days, to read and resend; a test of any event goes at once (`fctl webhooks`).
- **Agents that finish the job.** Follow-ups bring an agent back to the pull request it opened when someone who can write to the repository mentions `@fctl` or `@agent`, a check fails, the pull request conflicts with its base branch, or it merges or closes. Built-in review agents review every new commit of pull requests and hand their findings to the agent that opened the pull request.
- **Projects that run themselves** (experimental). Put a project, or a whole workspace, on autopilot with a direction: an agent plans the work, starts sessions to do it that merge their pull requests once checks pass (unless people leave merging to themselves), changes settings, secrets, repositories and schedules as far as it may, wakes at its check-in and whenever its sessions or people need it, and asks people for decisions and secrets without waiting for them.
- **Agents that learn.** A project memory of notes that each session's agent starts with and adds to, and a retrospective of each piece of work for the people who follow along.
- **Teams.** Workspaces with people, roles, runners, GitHub accounts, Linear workspaces, an audit log, two-factor sign-in and passkeys; projects with members, settings and secrets; sessions shared with others. An instance's admins can require Google of the people at their domains.
- **Subscriptions only.** API keys are stripped from every sandbox, a session must report a subscription credential, and a session pauses before it would draw on paid extra usage.
- **Yours to run.** The control plane runs on Cloudflare (a Rust → WebAssembly Worker with Durable Objects and D1) or in one container anywhere (`ghcr.io/hyperstructure/fctl-control`). Hosts dial out; nothing listens on your machines.

## How it fits together

```
web app · fctl CLI · HTTP API · Claude apps · Linear · GitHub webhooks
                         │
              control plane (an instance)      users, workspaces, projects, sessions' event logs,
                         │  (hosts dial out)    scheduling, credentials, GitHub App, Linear app
              fctl host on a machine (runner)  one sandbox per session: apple · lima · docker · firecracker · process
                         │
              fctl-agent + Claude Code         in the sandbox: journals events, pushes, reports git state
```

- The **control plane** (one per instance, such as app.fctl.sh) serves the API and the web app, keeps each session's event log, mints short-lived GitHub tokens, hands sessions to runners and relays messages. It never runs Claude itself.
- A **runner** is a machine that runs sessions. The `fctl host` service on it, the **host**, connects to the control plane, runs each of the runner's sessions in a **sandbox** made by its **driver**, and puts **fctl-agent** in it. One machine runs one host and is one runner: `fctl host` commands act on the machine they run on, while `fctl runners` and a workspace's Runners tab see runners from anywhere.
- **fctl-agent** supervises `claude -p` in stream-json mode, journals every event until the control plane acknowledges it, pushes branches, looks up pull requests, and answers the in-sandbox `fctl` commands (`fctl edit`, `fctl memory`, `fctl ticket`…) without any fctl credentials in the sandbox. In container and VM sandboxes it runs as root and Claude as the sandbox's user, whose `kill` can't stop it, unless the host sets `agent_as_root = false`: then it runs as that user too.

## Vocabulary

- **Instance**: one fctl deployment: a control plane and the runners connected to it. Its URL is what `fctl login` and `FCTL_SERVER` name (`https://app.fctl.sh`, or a self-hosted one).
- **Workspace** (`wsp_…`, `/w/<slug>`): the people who work together, their projects, the runners their sessions run on, the GitHub accounts and Linear workspaces they work in, and an audit log. A person is in at most five workspaces, or as many as the instance's admins choose (`fctl admin set --max-workspaces 50`, or `any`), and the primary instance owner in any number. Anyone creates one, unless the instance's admins keep that to themselves (`fctl admin set --members-create-workspaces off`).
- **Project** (`prj_…`, `/p/<slug>`, slugs are unique per instance): a primary GitHub repository (or none), more repositories of the same GitHub account (read only or read and write), and everything agents need: setup script, instructions, model and effort, the context size Claude compacts near, image, CPUs and memory, environment variables, secrets, idle timeout, GitHub access, follow-ups, ticket tracker, memory, schedules, review agents.
- **Slug**: a workspace's or project's address, unique on the instance among workspaces and among projects. A new one's comes from its name; when that one is taken or reserved (by fctl, like `new` and `settings`, or by an instance admin, like `home`), it gets a random ending of six hex digits, `my-app-829d34`. Nobody chooses a reserved slug with `--slug`.
- **Session** (`ses_…`, or `<project>#<number>` like `my-app#12`, URL `/s/<id>`): one agent working on one task: one Claude conversation in one sandbox on its own branch. A session has turns, a status, a transcript (its event log), pull requests, and a person it runs for, whose Claude subscription it uses.
- **Task**: the first message of a session. **Turn**: one round of Claude's work, from a message to the `result` that ends it. **Message**: what a person or tool sends a session at any time; it reaches the agent at its next step, and a stopped session resumes for it.
- **Agent**: Claude Code running in a session's sandbox. **Review agent**: an agent that reviews a pull request's commit and posts findings through fctl. In these docs "agent" means one of these unless it says otherwise.
- **Runner** (`rnr_…`): a machine registered with an instance, running the `fctl host` service, that runs sessions: several at once (4 by default), each in a sandbox of its own. It belongs to the person who registered it and runs the sessions of the workspaces it is added to: everyone's there (added by an admin) or only its owner's (added by a member, or `--personal`). One that enrolled with an enrollment token belongs to that workspace instead: it runs everyone's sessions there and no other workspace's, and its admins manage it; one that enrolled with a token a member made for their own sessions is that member's and runs only their sessions there.
- **Enrollment token** (`fctl_et_…`, id `enr_…`): a workspace's token with which machines enroll themselves as its runners without anyone signing in (`fctl host install --enroll`), as autoscaling creates them. Each machine gets a runner token of its own. A token has an expiry, a limit on its runners at once, and may make each runner wait for approval or remove runners that stay offline. Admins make them for everyone's sessions; any member makes one for their own (`--personal`), whose runners are theirs, count for Only on my runners and a Claude token kept on runners, and wait for their approval.
- **Pool**: the runners an enrollment token enrolled. They carry the token's labels (`--labels aws,large`) beside their `host.toml`'s, and take sessions as its placement says: `spread` (the least busy first) or `packed` (the busiest with room, the default for tokens that remove offline runners, so that idle machines can go). A project that sets `runner_labels` (`fctl projects set --runners large`) runs only on runners with them all, and its sessions wait for one, naming the pool, unless `--runner-fallback 15m` lets any runner take them after that long. `fctl runners pools` and `fctl runners demand` (`--json`, `--watch`, `--cloudwatch`) say what each pool needs now: its runners, slots, the sessions that wait for it, and `wanted`, the runners that would run them all.
- **Host**: the `fctl host` service on a runner, and the commands that install and look after it on that machine (`fctl host install|status|doctor|drain|uninstall`). It is not a group of runners: one machine is one runner, and its sandboxes all come from one driver. **Driver**: how a host makes sandboxes: `apple` (a lightweight VM per session, Apple silicon, macOS 26+), `lima` (a full VM), `docker` (a container; on macOS inside Docker's VM), `firecracker` (a microVM per session with a kernel of its own, Linux with KVM, chosen with `--driver firecracker`), `process` (no isolation, development only).
- **Sandbox**: the VM or container a session runs in. Its user is `agent`, the repository is at `~/workspace`, other repositories go in `~/repos/<owner>/<name>`, attachments in `~/attachments/`. A stopped session keeps its sandbox (72 hours by default) so a resume continues the same conversation, and a snapshot of its conversation and uncommitted work (encrypted, 30 days unless the workspace sets otherwise; in the control plane, or in a bucket of the organization's own where runners' `host.toml` has `[snapshots] url = "s3://bucket/prefix"`) so a resume on another runner does too.
- **Image**: what sandboxes start from: `ghcr.io/hyperstructure/sandbox:<version>` by default (Debian with git, gh, Python and uv, Rust, Node.js, TypeScript, Bun, Playwright with its browsers, Claude Code and fctl), or the project's own, or one built from a Dockerfile or devcontainer.json in its repository. An image on another base (Ubuntu, say) needs fctl, Claude Code, git, gh, bash and a user other than root, but no fctl-agent, which the host copies into each sandbox.
- **Claude connection** (`crd_…`): a person's Claude subscription credential: a full Claude login (Remote Control works), a long-lived token from `claude setup-token`, or a token kept on their runners that fctl never sees.
- **Access token** (`fctl_pat_…`, id `tok_…`): a token for scripts, CI, bots and other agents, optionally limited to reading, running sessions or everything, to some projects or workspaces, and in what its sessions' agents may do on GitHub.
- **Service account** (`fctl_svc_…`, id `sva_…`): a workspace's credential for a program of its own (a portal where people start agents, a chat bot, a script). Each request names the person it acts for (`Fctl-On-Behalf-Of: <address or usr_…>`, `fctl --on-behalf-of`), and the session it starts is theirs: on their Claude subscription, within their roles, followed by them. It acts only for members who allowed it, unless the instance's admins turned asking off; without a person it reads the workspace's projects, sessions and schedules, and runs schedules for the people they run for. Its admins make them; it works while the admin who made its secret is still one.
- **GitHub access** of a session: `push` (commit, push, open pull requests), `comment` (review, comment, label, resolve review threads; push nothing) or `read` (read only). The most a session gets is what its project and the token that starts it allow.
- **Follow-up**: a message from fctl that brings an agent back to a pull request its session opened: `comments`, `checks`, `conflicts`, `closed`.
- **Webhook** (`whk_…`, events `evt_…`, deliveries `whd_…`): an `https://` address fctl posts a workspace's events to (for all its projects or some; a project's own for its events), with the events it wants, whose sessions' (`started_by`), and a `whsec_…` secret that signs each request (`webhook-id`, `webhook-timestamp`, `webhook-signature`); each request names its `workspace` and `project` by id.
- **Schedule** (`sch_…`, runs `srn_…`): a task fctl starts sessions for on its own: on a cron expression in a time zone, once at a time, each time an event happens on GitHub in the project's repositories (`issue_opened`, `issue_labeled`, `pull_request_opened`, `pull_request_merged`, `release_published`, `checks_failed`), or only when asked (by a person or a tool).
- **Autopilot** (experimental): an agent that runs a project, or its whole workspace, on its own, from a direction people give it and change at any time, on the subscription of whoever put it on, as whom it acts; someone else who changes how much it works, or resumes it, runs it on theirs from then on, unless its owner keeps it on their own (`fctl autopilot set --keep-owner on`, for a project whose people they all trust). It works in sessions of its own in its project (a fresh one, which starts from its plan, log and files, after 12 hours, once its context holds as many tokens as people choose: `fctl autopilot set --handoff-at 250k`, when people ask: `fctl autopilot wake --fresh`, or when the runner that keeps its sandbox drains or is gone), starts sessions to do the work (as many at once as people allow, counting those queued, starting, working, paused on a usage limit or still stopping and one it just messaged, not one that ended its turn to wait for its background work; at the limit, `fctl send` to one that rests holds the message, `aph_…`, and fctl sends it as soon as one of its sessions ends its turn, stops or fails, those held in the order sent, listed and taken back with `fctl autopilot held`; each wake says the start of what each said as its turn ended, or why it ended its turn without a word where fctl knows (Claude Code cut off twice, an interrupt, a message mid-turn), and what people wrote to them, which doesn't wake it itself; a pull request of one merging or closing wakes it, and once one merged, the checks on its base branch ending wake it again with how they went, so that it needs no script to wait for main to go green), attaches files to their tasks and messages (`fctl run --attach`, `fctl send --attach`: one people sent it, one it made, or one sent in another of its sessions, which `fctl files get <ref> <name>` downloads; an older sandbox image's `fctl` can't, and it passes screenshots on as links it publishes with `fctl publish` instead), looks after the sessions people start there (asking them before it helps get a pull request of theirs merged, with a session of its own), keeps a plan and a log, and files that its next sessions get back in their new sandbox (`fctl autopilot files put/get/rm`: text such as the scripts it relies on, templates and a draft until it sends it, as fctl keeps the text it sent, 256 KB each and 4 MB in all, which people read on its tab; its brief and `fctl autopilot files` mark those its plan doesn't name, and a fresh session of its own goes through them, as it does once it keeps more than 25), keeps the project's memory as its sessions do and deletes its notes stale for over a day itself, without asking, once its brief says they crowd the memory (900 of the 1,000 notes a project keeps, stale ones included: `fctl memory delete --stale`), reads where things stand in its brief (`fctl autopilot brief`, or parts of it: `--only sessions,people,asks`), asks people questions and for secrets (`fctl autopilot ask`, `apa_…`; a question about one of its sessions, `--session crm#12`, links to it, and the files people attach to their answer, `fctl autopilot answer --attach`, go to that session) and takes their notes (`apn_…`). Its workspace's admins let projects have one. It is token hungry: several sessions at once, kept going on their own, drain a Claude plan's usage quickly, so a fresh build on Pro can reach the five-hour limit, where its sessions pause until the limit resets; Max and Ultra plans are usually enough, as the Autopilot tab and the workspace's setting say.
- **Ticket tracker**: where a project's agents read and write tickets: GitHub Issues (of every repository they write to, or one), Linear teams (one or several, each optionally narrowed to one of its Linear projects), or none. In a sandbox, `fctl ticket` reaches it.
- **Memory** (`mem_…`): a project's notes for the agents of later sessions. **Retrospective** (`rtr_…`): how a piece of work ended (`completed`, `partial`, `blocked`), what was done, the approach, what got in the way, and what a future agent should know.
- **Agent Floor**: the web app's home page: the task box and every active session.
- **Remote Control**: Claude Code's link to the Claude apps; sessions on a full Claude login show up in claude.ai/code and the Claude apps of the person they run for.
- **Published screenshot**: an image an agent publishes with `fctl publish` at an unguessable link, to show in a pull request (off unless the instance and the project allow it).
- **Drain**: a runner that drains takes no new sessions while the ones it has carry on.

## Roles

- **Instance**: `owner` (the primary instance owner, one), `admin` (people, invitations, allowlist, runners, GitHub installations, instance settings, reserved slugs; not inside workspaces they aren't in), `member`.
- **Workspace**: the primary admin (one; hands the role over before leaving), `admin` (people, roles, runners, GitHub and Linear connections, settings; creates projects; owns every project), `member`. A **base role** (`none`, `viewer`, `editor`, `maintainer`; new workspaces: `editor`) gives every member that role in every project.
- **Project**: `owner` (everything, including deleting it and turning review agents on), `maintainer` (settings, secrets, members, schedules of others), `editor` (start sessions, message agents, keep memory), `viewer` (read sessions). A member's role is the higher of their project role and the base role.
- **Session**: `owner` (who started it, while they may still start sessions in the project, and the project's maintainers and owners: stop, resume, archive, share), `editor` (message and interrupt), `viewer` (read). Sessions can be shared with people in the same workspace, as viewers, editors or owners.
- **Access token**: `read` (like a viewer), `run` (like an editor, and it stops and resumes the sessions it started), `full` (whatever its person may in its projects). A limited token never reaches the account, workspaces' people and settings, Claude connections, other tokens or administration.
- **Admin token** (`fctl_adm_…`, id `adt_…`; self-hosted instances whose deployment sets `FCTL_ADMIN_TOKENS=1`, never app.fctl.sh): an instance admin's, for programs that provision people. It acts as that admin on the admin API's people endpoints alone: creates accounts (`POST /api/v1/admin/users`), reads one with their workspaces and projects (`GET /api/v1/admin/users/{id or address}`), changes names, primary address, commit email and status (`PATCH`), sets their picture and the Claude token their sessions run on (`PUT …/avatar`, `PUT …/claude`), adds them to any workspace and project or takes them out (`PUT`/`DELETE …/workspaces/{workspace}`, `…/projects/{project}`), and deletes them. A new account has no password (set one with `password`, or the link `fctl admin reset-link` makes, except where Google is required for its domain): where the instance has Google sign-in and Google hosts the address (Workspace or Gmail), the person's first Google sign-in links Google to it. It changes no roles and never the primary instance owner's account; only the primary owner's tokens change admins'. CLI: `fctl admin tokens create NAME`, then `FCTL_TOKEN=fctl_adm_… fctl admin users create|show|set|add|remove`.
- **Sign-in rules** (instance admins: Admin → Sign-in, `fctl admin sign-in require acme.com acme.dev`, `PATCH /api/v1/admin/settings` with `sign_in`): the people with an address at those domains sign in with Google alone, as that address (a Google Workspace account's): passwords, passkeys alone (unless `--passkeys`) and personal Google accounts stop working, and saving it deletes their browser sessions, CLI sign-ins, access tokens and admin tokens made another way, before the rule too; their next Google sign-in links Google and takes their password. Closing their Google account stops their next sign-in, not their sessions: disable their account too. The primary instance owner keeps every way in, for when Google is down; a rule that would sign out the admin who saves it waits until they sign in with Google. `fctl admin sign-in` shows whom each covers; `POST /api/v1/admin/sign-in/preview` says what a change would do; `fctl admin set --self-sign-up off` makes signing in make no accounts (only invitations, allowed addresses and admin tokens). Someone whose Workspace account was recreated at the same address: `fctl admin unlink ada@acme.com` signs them out everywhere, then their next Google sign-in links the new one; an address handed to someone else calls for `fctl admin disable` instead. A CLI refused by a rule signs in again with `fctl login`. **A workspace's own requirement** (its admins: `fctl workspaces set -w acme --require-google acme.com,acme.dev`, Settings → Access, `PATCH /api/v1/workspaces/{id}` with `sign_in`): members in it as an address there open it only signed in with Google as that address (`sign_in_blocked` on the workspace otherwise); others sign in as before.
- **Service account**: as the person a request names, what an access token that runs sessions does, in its workspace's projects (start sessions, message, interrupt, stop and resume theirs, run schedules, keep memory), within that person's roles; as nobody, it reads them. Never the account, people, settings, secrets, tokens or live connections (`/ws`): read events with `fctl logs` or `GET /api/v1/sessions/{id}/events`.

## Session lifecycle

```
queued → provisioning → preparing → running ⇄ idle → stopping → stopped
                                       │                         failed (any time)
                                       └→ paused (usage limit; resumes on its own)
```

- `queued`: waiting for a runner of its workspace that is online, has a free slot, runs its image and size, runs this person's sessions and whose driver can start sandboxes (Docker running, say). `status_reason` says why it waits ("Waiting for a runner: …", "Waiting for studio, whose docker driver isn't ready: …"): a busy runner frees up by itself, and a session starts once a driver is ready, but no runner online, or none that allows its image or size, takes a person; a driver that isn't ready takes its runner's owner (`fctl runners` says why).
- `provisioning` → `preparing`: the host makes the sandbox; the agent clones the repository, creates the branch and runs the project's setup script.
- `running`: a turn is under way. `idle`: the turn ended and the agent waits for a message (`status_reason` "Waiting for a message"), or for its background tasks ("Waiting for 2 background tasks"), whose results Claude takes in a turn of its own.
- An idle session stops after the project's idle timeout (10 minutes unless set; `fctl projects set --idle-timeout`). Background work keeps it up for at most an hour after its last turn. `stopped` keeps the sandbox: a message to a stopped session resumes it on the same runner, with Claude's conversation and anything uncommitted. If that runner is gone or busy, it resumes at once on another runner in a new sandbox, restored from the snapshot its agent saved as it stopped (`fctl show` says what it holds); without one (the workspace keeps none: `fctl workspaces set --snapshots off`, or the runner went without a word), after 10 minutes, from the pushed branch with a new conversation. `fctl workspaces snapshots` says what a workspace's snapshots take, with fctl and in its runners' buckets.
- `paused`: the person's plan hit a usage limit (or the turn would have drawn on paid extra usage); it continues by itself when the limit resets (`resume_at`).
- `failed`: something went wrong (`status_reason` says what). Only a resume (`fctl resume`, on the resumer's subscription) restarts a failed session; a message doesn't.
- A message keeps a session on the subscription it ran on, a paused one too. `fctl take-over SESSION` (**Continue on my subscription**) moves one that is paused, idle or stopped to your Claude connection for its workspace (another of your own connections too): it starts again there, in the same conversation. An autopilot moves its own sessions to its owner's connection as it wakes, once someone takes it over or its owner chooses or connects another.
- A runner that goes away leaves its agents working; after ten minutes the session shows as stopped and a message resumes it elsewhere, unless the runner comes back first.
- A runner short of disk tells its sessions in notices (`fctl logs --json`: `kind` `notice`, `.data.code`): `runner_low_on_disk` (`warn`) below the floor its host keeps (`min_free_disk_gb`, 20 GiB by default), `runner_out_of_disk` (`error`) below 2 GiB, when the agent's writes are about to fail, and `runner_disk_ok` (`info`) once it has had room for ten minutes. On Firecracker runners the host then pauses the sandbox (`sandbox_paused`) and resumes it once there is room (`sandbox_resumed`): the agent waits, losing nothing, and its status doesn't change. `agent_restarted` says the host started fctl-agent again while the disk was short. A session stuck on a full runner needs someone to free space there: report it rather than wait.
- A sandbox short of memory says so in notices too: `memory_nearly_out` (`warn`) when it is 85% full while the agent works, naming what holds the most, and `memory_killed` (`warn`) when the kernel killed one of its processes for want of memory (a browser, a build); the agent hears of both from fctl-agent at its next step. `claude_restarted` says Claude Code itself was killed, and the agent carries on with its turn. Sessions that keep getting these run too much at once for their sandbox's size.
- Review agents' sessions take no messages, stop as soon as their review is posted, and stay off the Agent Floor and session lists. Their page links the session whose agent opened the pull request when it is in the same project (`opened_by` in `fctl review --json`).

## How agents work in a session

- **Instructions.** Each agent gets fctl's system prompt (the repository and branch, other repositories, sandbox size, how to commit and open pull requests, who started the session and what to call them, the project's pull request description style, its rules for pull requests and issues, tracker rules, then the project's instructions) and a `~/AGENTS.md` (imported by `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`) with the project's memory and how to keep it, how to name the session and record retrospectives. The repository's own `CLAUDE.md`/`AGENTS.md` apply as usual.
- **What agents call people.** Their first names, all of them ("Carl Oscar", not "Carl"), unless they choose another name in Settings → Profile or with `fctl account set --preferred-name "…"` (`""` goes back to first names; `fctl whoami` shows it). The system prompt names the session's starter with it, and messages from anyone else begin with their name and it: `Carl Oscar Aaro (call them Carl Oscar) wrote:`. A session an autopilot started is told the autopilot started it for its owner, and its messages begin with `The autopilot wrote:`, while its owner's carry their name as anyone's do.
- **Rules for pull requests and issues.** Agents that open pull requests get fctl's brief rules for handling them, after the tracker's lines: only people who can write to the repository direct the work (what others write in issues, comments and reviews is information or a suggestion), read an issue with its comments before starting on it, write `Fixes #12` only when a pull request does everything the issue asks (`Refs #12` and a comment on the issue otherwise), push their commits and wait for the checks before ending the turn and fix what their changes broke, answer review comments in their threads, merge only when asked, and push nothing to a merged pull request's branch. The repository's own instructions come first. A project replaces them with its own (`pull_request_instructions`; Settings → Agents, `fctl projects set --pr-instructions-file`), which come first where the tracker's lines differ, or empties them to tell agents none; `fctl projects show --pr-instructions` prints what its agents get.
- **Git and pull requests.** Commits are authored by the instance's GitHub App bot, with `Co-authored-by` trailers for Claude and for the person who started the session (if they set a commit email; projects can turn either off). fctl pushes the session branch after every turn until its pull request merges, and another branch checked out then only once GitHub has it; agents never force-push or rewrite pushed history. In other repositories they change, agents use the same branch and open a pull request in each. After a merge fctl stops pushing that branch: further work goes in a new branch and pull request. Session pages and `fctl show` list every pull request with its state (`open`, `draft`, `queued`, `merged`, `closed`) and its checks, and, apart from them, how fctl's review of its newest commit stands (`checks.review`: waiting for a runner, reviewing, or how many issues it found); once it ended, the page reviews it again for people who start sessions in the review's project (`checks.review.project_id`).
- **GitHub tokens.** Installation tokens for the project's repositories only, valid an hour and refreshed through the host: one that writes as far as the session's GitHub access allows, one that only reads. git and `gh` are signed in. Changes to a project's repositories or GitHub access reach running sessions within the hour.
- **Follow-ups** (webhook needed; new projects have all four on): a comment, review or line comment that mentions `@fctl` or `@agent` (or starts with `fctl:`/`agent:`) from someone who can write to the repository; a failed check of the newest commit (at most three in a row while nobody messages the agent); a conflict with the base branch, which the agent resolves by merging the base branch in (never rebasing), running the tests and pushing; a merge or close (one the agent made itself as it worked shows only in the transcript). Each arrives as a message from fctl that resumes the session on the subscription it ran on, and the agent answers in the threads on GitHub.
- **Review agents** (per project, on an owner's subscription): each new commit of a pull request in the repositories the project writes to gets a review: an `eyes` reaction, an `fctl review` check, a summary comment and findings on the lines, posted as the instance's review app (`fctl-review` on app.fctl.sh) where it's installed on the account, else as its GitHub App (`fctl workspaces review-app` says which, and gives a workspace's admins the links that install it). Owners skip repositories another project reviews already (`fctl review settings --skip-repos acme/shared-lib`), whose pull requests then get no review in theirs; new ones are reviewed until skipped. Drafts get reviews too until owners turn them off (`--drafts off`): then a draft gets its review when it's marked ready for review, or when someone asks. With `--description-summary on`, the agent first sums each pull request up at the end of its description (how risky it looks, what it does, what deserves a closer look, in a GitHub alert between `<!-- FCTL_REVIEW_SUMMARY -->` marks), in place of an earlier review's; fctl writes it and leaves the rest of the description as it is. Pull requests from people who can't write to the repository, and from apps other than the ones the owners chose (Dependabot by default), are reviewed only when someone asks (`fctl review start`). When an fctl agent opened the pull request, its session gets the findings to fix or answer, with earlier reviews' findings still open, which come alone when a review finds nothing new and the agent hasn't heard of each as it stands (at most five reviews in a row while no person messages it, or as many as the owners chose from one to ten: `--rounds 3`; then the session's page, under the pull request, continues for as many rounds again, the held findings first: `fctl review pass-on my-app#12`). Findings that went to no session, since none listed the pull request yet, go to the session that opened it once it lists it.
- **In-sandbox commands** (through fctl-agent, no sign-in): `fctl edit --title … --description …` (name the session), `fctl ask "…" -o "…" -o "…"` (ask the people who follow the session for input, with answers to click, then end the turn; their next message answers it; `--withdraw` takes it back), `fctl memory` / `fctl memory add|stale|duplicate`, `fctl retro` / `fctl retro update|list`, `fctl ticket …`, `fctl publish FILE` (screenshots for pull requests; `gh pr edit --attach` fails with the app's token), `fctl resolve PRRT_…` (resolve review threads, for agents that comment), `fctl id-token -a AUDIENCE` (an identity token: below), and for review agents `fctl review threads`, `fctl review summarize FILE` and `fctl review submit FILE`.
- **Identity tokens.** `fctl id-token -a https://api.example.com` mints an OpenID Connect (OIDC) ID token that the workspace's issuer (`{instance}/oidc/{wsp_…}`) signs, for that audience alone, for 10 minutes: it says whom the session runs for (`user_id`, `user_email`), its workspace, project, session, runner, branch, `github_access` and `started_by`, with `sub` = `project:prj_…:user:usr_…` (`--subject` chooses other parts). Send it as the service asks, usually `Authorization: Bearer …`, and never print or commit it; `--claims` shows what it says. Services check it with the issuer's keys (`/.well-known/jwks.json`). Where the project reaches AWS, Google Cloud or Azure (Settings → Identity OIDC, `fctl projects set --aws-role / --gcp-provider / --azure-client`), fctl-agent keeps their tokens in the sandbox and sets `AWS_ROLE_ARN` and `AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE`, `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS`, or `AZURE_CLIENT_ID` and `AZURE_FEDERATED_TOKEN_FILE`: their CLIs and SDKs sign in on their own. Review agents mint none; a project's maintainers can turn them off.
- **What a sandbox has.** The project's environment variables and secrets, `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` (a stand-in where the session's person keeps their token out of sandboxes), `FCTL_SESSION_ID`, `FCTL_SESSION_URL`, `FCTL_SANDBOX_CPUS`, `FCTL_SANDBOX_MEMORY_MB`, outbound network, sudo. No fctl credentials, no API keys, no GitHub App key.

## Claude credentials and usage

- Each person connects their own subscription (Pro or Max) in Settings → Claude or with `fctl claude connect` (paste a `claude setup-token` token; lasts a year, so sessions run around the clock without a new sign-in, which is why Settings recommends it; no Remote Control or claude.ai connectors), `fctl claude connect --on-runners` after `fctl host claude set-token` on each of their runners (the same kind of token, which never reaches fctl; their sessions then run only on those runners), or `fctl claude connect --login` (full login through a host: one of theirs, or, when none is online, one that runs their sessions, which the app and CLI name first, since its host sees the login and could swap in a Claude account of its own; Remote Control and claude.ai connectors, but Claude ends it after a while and its sessions stop until they sign in again).
- A session runs on the connection of the person it runs for: who started it (or resumed or took it over last; a schedule's owner; review agents' operator; whoever delegated a Linear ticket; the access token's person). Changing a schedule, or how review agents review, runs it on the subscription of whoever changes it from then on: nobody changes what runs on someone else's subscription. A member chooses which connection each workspace's sessions use (`fctl workspaces claude <connection> -w <workspace>`).
- `fctl claude status` shows each connection's plan usage (five-hour window, week, per-model week) as sessions last reported it, and `ultra` for Claude's Ultra plan, which has no five-hour window; when Claude last answered it; and when a long-lived token runs out: a year after `claude setup-token` made it (`fctl claude connect --made-at 2026-11-20`; without it fctl counts the year from the connection and says "around"; connecting the same token again keeps its date). Sessions pause at a limit and resume when it resets.
- **When a connection stops working.** Claude refuses a revoked or expired token in the sessions that run on it; once it did in as many sessions as the instance says (2 by default, `fctl admin set --claude-refusals`) since it last answered it, fctl marks it ended, as it marks a login Claude won't renew, and sessions run on the person's other connection if one works. fctl tells the person 30 and 7 days before a token runs out and as soon as one stops working: by email where the instance sends it, under the connection in Settings → Claude, and on the Agent Floor in its last week.
- **What admins see** (Claude seats in organizations): a workspace's admins see on its People tab, and with `fctl workspaces members -w acme --claude [--problems] [--expiring 30d] [--json]`, each member's connection there: its state (none, unused, works, ended), plan, kind and who set it (an admin token), when Claude last answered it, when its token runs out, whether their sessions wait for a usage limit, and how often their sessions there paused on limits in 7 and 30 days; never a token, its account or its label. The instance's admins choose the most workspaces' admins may see (`fctl admin set --claude-oversight details|readiness|off --claude-limit-pauses on|off`) and whether they see everyone's themselves (`--claude-instance-view on`, then Admin → People and `fctl admin claude`); each workspace chooses within it and how its admins hear by email (`fctl workspaces set --claude-oversight … --claude-limit-pauses … --claude-admin-email weekly|each|off`, weekly by default). Members read what their admins see in the workspace's Settings → You. API: `GET /api/v1/workspaces/{id}/claude`, `GET /api/v1/admin/claude`.
- **Keeping the token out of sandboxes** (experimental, off by default): `fctl claude set --stand-in on` (Settings → Claude) gives Claude a stand-in that Anthropic refuses, and the host of the runner puts the person's token in as Claude's requests leave for `api.anthropic.com`, so agents can neither read the token nor send it anywhere. It applies to the sessions that start afterwards, to every connection of theirs; Remote Control and claude.ai connectors may not work with it. Turning it off may need confirming it's them.

## Driving fctl from an agent or a script

Install and sign in:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://fctl.sh/install | sh      # or: brew install hyperstructure/tap/fctl
export FCTL_SERVER=https://app.fctl.sh      # the instance
export FCTL_TOKEN=fctl_pat_…                # an access token a person made for this
fctl whoami                                  # who it acts as, and what the token may do
```

- A program that starts sessions for other people (an organization's portal or bot) uses a workspace's service account instead: `FCTL_TOKEN=fctl_svc_… fctl run -p my-app --on-behalf-of ada@example.com -d "…"`. A refusal because it can't act for the person (not a member, hasn't allowed it, disabled, two-factor not set up) has `"field": "on_behalf_of"`; one because they lack the role there (editor, to start sessions) is `forbidden`, and a project they can't see `not_found`. Each says why: show them the message. `fctl sessions --mine` lists the sessions it started.
- Prefer an access token limited to the job over a person's sign-in: `fctl token "Nightly triage" --access run -p my-app --github triage --days 30` (a person runs it; it prints the token once). `fctl login` needs a person to approve the device in a browser (`--no-browser` prints the link). A personal agent asks its person which of the two they want first (Signing in from a personal agent, below).
- Name sessions by id (`ses_…`, also in URLs) in scripts: `my-app#12` only finds the project's latest 200 sessions.
- `--json` prints one JSON document on stdout, in the API's shapes (`fctl run -d --json` prints the new session, `.id` is its id). `fctl logs --json` is the exception: one event per line (JSON Lines), with or without `-f`; use `jq -s` to read it as an array.
- `fctl logs SESSION --last-turn` prints only the last message to the agent and what followed (read from the transcript's end, so it stays quick on a long session): how its latest turn went, without the rest.
- Files go with a task or message (`fctl run --attach FILE`, `fctl send SESSION --attach FILE`: up to 10, of at most 20 MB each). `fctl files list SESSION` lists those sent in a session, and `fctl files get SESSION NAME` (or `--all`, `--dir DIR`) downloads them, to pass one on to another session; it writes over no file already there without `--force`.
- Exit codes: 0 success; 1 an error (the message on stderr, as text even with `--json`); 2 a usage error (unknown flag, missing argument). Check the exit code; don't parse stderr.
- Commands that take a project use `-p`, else the default from `fctl projects use`. Commands that take a workspace use `-w`, else `fctl workspaces use`, else your only one.
- A turn is over when a new `result` event appears in the transcript. Right after a message the status can still say `idle`, before the agent takes it, so count `result` events rather than watch the status. A `failed` session takes no turn until someone resumes it, and a `paused` one until its person's usage limit resets.

The core loop:

```sh
id=$(fctl run -p my-app -d --json "Fix the flaky login test and open a pull request" | jq -r .id)

turns() { fctl logs "$1" --json | jq -s '[.[] | select(.kind == "claude" and .data.type == "result")] | length'; }
wait_turn() {   # waits until the session has more than $2 finished turns, or can't go on
  while [ "$(turns "$1")" -le "$2" ]; do
    case $(fctl show "$1" --json | jq -r .status) in failed|paused) return 1 ;; esac
    sleep 20
  done
}

wait_turn "$id" 0
fctl logs "$id" --json | jq -s -r '[.[] | select(.kind == "claude" and .data.type == "result")] | last | .data.result'
fctl show "$id" --json | jq '{status, status_reason, branch, pull_requests}'

n=$(turns "$id"); fctl send "$id" "Also add a regression test"; wait_turn "$id" "$n"
```

A session that stays `queued` says why in `status_reason` (no runner online, no runner allows its image, its person's runners are offline…): report it rather than wait forever.

## Signing in from a personal agent

Personal agents that work for one person across their apps, such as [Grok Bot](https://x.ai/bot), [Claude Duet](https://claude.com/product/claude-duet), [Meta Muse](https://ai.meta.com/muse/), [Wabi](https://wabi.ai) and OpenAI's [ChatGPT Dots](https://chatgpt.com/features/dots), drive fctl as above. Their person is there to answer, so before signing in, ask them which of two kinds of access they want to give you, unless their request already says:

- **A full sign-in**: anything they can do in fctl, in every workspace and project, with their account, Claude connections and access tokens. Run `fctl login app.fctl.sh --no-browser` (or their own instance's address): it prints a link and a code, then waits up to ten minutes and returns once they approve, so run it in the background, or wherever you read its output before it returns, and without `--json`, with which it prints neither link nor code. Show them the link and the code; they open the link, check that the page shows the same code, and approve. Revoking the sign-in in their Settings → Security signs you out at once.
- **A token for one project**: what an editor does in that project: start sessions and steer their agents, run its schedules, keep its memory, and read its sessions and retrospectives. It reaches nothing outside the project: not their other projects, their workspaces' people, settings and runners, their account or their other tokens. They make it in Settings → Access tokens (New access token: Run sessions, Only some, the project, an expiry) or with `fctl token "Personal agent" --access run -p xyz123 --days 30`, and give it to you: keep it in `FCTL_TOKEN`, with `FCTL_SERVER`, and don't repeat it in the conversation. Add `--github comment`, `--github triage` or `--github read` to keep its sessions' agents from pushing. `--access full` (Everything) in place of `run` also changes the project's settings, secrets, members and schedules, as far as their role there allows, but takes no `--github`: it could change the settings that say what the project's agents may do.

What they ask is a hint. "I want to use the fctl.sh CLI to manage the xyz123 project" names one project, so they most likely want a token for xyz123 alone: not a full sign-in, nor a token for every project of the workspace xyz123 is in (`-w`). Suggest `--access run -p xyz123`, or `--access full -p xyz123` if they also want you to change its settings. When they name more projects, or a workspace, the token takes them all (`-p` repeated, `-w`); a full sign-in is for when they want you to reach their account, or their workspaces' people, settings and runners. Either way, the sessions you start run as them, on their Claude subscription. More in [fctl for agents](https://fctl.sh/docs/agents.md#from-a-personal-agent).

## Things to avoid

- **`fctl run` without `-d` never exits on its own.** It follows the session and reconnects forever, also after the session stops, so a tool call that runs it hangs until it is killed. Always pass `-d` (`--detach`) in scripts and tool calls.
- **`fctl attach` and `fctl logs -f` don't exit when the session ends.** `fctl logs -f` and `fctl attach --read-only` exit at once only if the session had already stopped or failed when they connected; `fctl attach` never does. Use `fctl logs` (without `-f`) and `fctl show`, or wrap them in `timeout`. `fctl attach` is for people at a terminal.
- **`fctl run` and `fctl send` without message text read stdin until it closes**, so they hang where stdin stays open. Give the text as an argument or with `-f FILE` (`fctl run`), or pipe it in explicitly.
- **Don't retry `fctl send` blindly**: each call is a new message. It already tries again, without delivering twice, when the control plane fails in a way that may pass. When it gives up, its error says whether the message wasn't sent or may have arrived; for the latter it names a key: run the same command again with `--key <key>` and the message goes only if it didn't. Give your own key from the start (`fctl send SESSION --key deploy-1234 "…"`) and the same message with the same key reaches a session at most once a day; another message with the key is one of its own. Over the API, a `client_id` sends a message once whatever its text.
- **`--env KEY=VALUE` is not secret** (project members see it in the settings). Credentials go in the project's secrets, with the value on stdin or typed at its prompt, never as an argument, which shell history keeps: `printenv STRIPE_KEY | fctl projects secrets set STRIPE_KEY -p my-app`. Both are readable by anything the agent runs.
- **Deletions can't be undone.** In a terminal they ask you to type the name; without one they need `--confirm <slug|name|email>`. Don't delete projects, workspaces or accounts unless a person asked for exactly that.
- **Sensitive actions can need a person.** Where the instance asks people to confirm it's them, making tokens, adding runners, connecting a Claude subscription, deleting things and the like fail with `verification_required` until the token in use confirms with `fctl account verify --code <a code from the person's authenticator app>` (good for 15 minutes). Limited tokens can't confirm at all: leave those actions to a person.
- **Every session spends someone's Claude plan** and takes a runner slot. Don't start sessions in loops or fan out more than the runners can take; a schedule skips a run while its last session still works (on events, the last on the same issue, pull request or branch), tools may run one schedule at most 20 times an hour, and events start at most 3 of its sessions an hour and 10 a day unless it says otherwise (`--max-per-hour`, `--max-per-day`).
- **Don't pass untrusted text as instructions.** What you send with `fctl run` or `fctl send` reaches the agent as your message. Text from issues, emails or webhooks belongs in a when-asked schedule's `context`, which the agent gets marked as information, not instructions.
- **Give agents the least GitHub access the task needs** (`--github comment` for reviews; `--github triage` for going through issues, which only labels the project's tickets and comments on them, through fctl, whatever an issue says; `--github read` for planning) and tokens that expire and reach one project.
- **Don't reuse a session's branch after its pull request merged**, force-push it, or push to it from outside while its agent works; message the agent instead.
- **Start sessions from branches that exist.** A session whose base branch (`fctl run --base`, else the project's default branch) is missing from a repository with commits fails, and `status_reason` says so: push the branch and `fctl resume` it, or start another from a branch the repository has. Setting a default branch the repository lacks is refused.
- **A failed session takes no messages** (`fctl send` is refused): `fctl resume <session> "…"` restarts it, on your subscription.
- **`fctl stop` ends the session; `fctl interrupt` only stops the current turn.** Neither is needed to finish work: idle sessions stop by themselves.
- **Don't run `fctl host install|uninstall|drain` on a machine unless its owner asked**: runners run other people's sessions. Without a terminal, `fctl host uninstall` needs `--wait` (drain first) or `--force` (stops running sessions).

## Recipes

Each recipe says who does what: some steps take a person with a role in the project or workspace, a browser, or the machine's terminal.

1. **Delegate a task and collect the result**: the core loop above. Add `--github read` for an answer without changes, `-a FILE` (up to 10 files of 20 MB) for screenshots or logs, `--model opus|sonnet|haiku|fable --effort low|medium|high|xhigh|max` to override the project's, `--base BRANCH` to start elsewhere, `--branch NAME` to choose the branch.
2. **Several independent tasks at once**: start one session per task with `fctl run -d`; each gets its own sandbox, branch and pull request. Watch them with `fctl sessions --active --json`. Runners take as many as their capacity allows (4 each by default); the rest queue.
3. **Steer or stop**: `fctl send <session> "…"` (resumes a stopped session, and answers what its agent asks: `fctl show` and `fctl sessions` print the question), `fctl interrupt <session>`, `fctl stop <session>`, `fctl resume <session> "…"`. Its owner changes the model or effort level its agent works at from its next step, and its next run's: `fctl edit <session> --effort medium` (plan at xhigh, build at medium) keeps Claude's prompt cache where Claude sends the level with each turn; `--model sonnet` makes its next step read the whole conversation again without the cache.
4. **From any tool (issue tracker, chat bot, deploy pipeline, n8n/Zapier/Make)**: a person sets up a schedule that runs when asked and a token that runs sessions in that project, then the tool posts what it knows:
   ```sh
   fctl schedules add "Triage an issue" -p my-app --when-asked --github triage \
     -m "Triage the issue that comes with this: label it, say what is missing, link duplicates."
   fctl token "Issue triage" --access run -p my-app --github triage --days 90
   curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $FCTL_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -d '{"context": "Issue #41: The login page hangs on Safari…"}' \
     "$FCTL_SERVER/api/v1/schedules/sch_…/runs"          # context: at most 20,000 characters
   ```
   The answer is the run, with the session it started (`.session.id`). From a shell: `fctl schedules run sch_… --context-file -`. For what happens on GitHub itself, no tool is needed: a schedule that runs on an event (below) starts from fctl's own webhook.
5. **Recurring work**: `fctl schedules add "Weekly dependencies" -p my-app --cron "0 9 * * 1" --tz Europe/Stockholm -m "Update the dependencies with patch or minor releases, run the tests and open a pull request."` Once: `--at 2h` or `--at 2026-10-30T16:00+01:00`. Five-field cron or `@daily`/`@weekly`…, at most every 15 minutes, `--tz` defaults to the machine's zone (set it in CI), `--paused` to set one up stopped, `--hide-sessions` to keep its sessions off session lists (the Agent Floor, the sidebar, the project's sessions, `fctl sessions` without `--hidden`; its runs list them). Runs go on the schedule owner's subscription; `fctl schedules runs sch_…` says what each run started or why not. A run an autopilot asks for (`fctl schedules run`) is one of its sessions, as those it starts with `fctl run` are: it counts toward its session limit, and wakes it as they do.
6. **On events on GitHub**: `fctl schedules add "Triage new issues" -p my-app --on issue-opened --github triage -m "Triage the issue: label it, and ask for what is missing to act on it."`. `--on` takes `issue-opened`, `issue-labeled` (with `--label fctl`: label an issue to hand it to an agent; only a label a person who may triage the repository adds counts, not an app's, fctl's agents' or an issue template's), `pr-opened`, `pr-merged`, `release` or `checks-failed` (all checks of a branch's newest commit ended, one failed; the default branch unless `--branch`). `--repo owner/name` (one of the project's; default those its agents write to), `--label`, `--branch` and `--by anyone|writers|agents` narrow it down (default anyone, but writers for `pr-opened`). One that anyone on GitHub can start (issues opened, pull requests opened by anyone) runs at triage unless `--github` says more. Each event starts one run, on the owner's subscription, at most 3 an hour and 10 a day unless `--max-per-hour` and `--max-per-day` say otherwise (up to 100 and 1,000), whose agent gets what GitHub said of it after the task as information, not instructions; `fctl schedules runs` names the issue, pull request, release or commit of each. It needs the instance's GitHub App subscribed to the event (Issues for issues): `fctl schedules` says when it isn't.
6. **Review pull requests**: a project owner turns on review agents: `fctl review settings -p my-app --on --model opus --effort high` (instructions: `--instructions-file review.md`; apps whose pull requests start reviews: `--bots dependabot,renovate`; repositories another project reviews: `--skip-repos acme/shared-lib`; drafts only once they're ready: `--drafts off`; a summary at the end of each description: `--description-summary on`; how many reviews in a row reach the agent that opened the pull request before fctl pauses for a person: `--rounds 3`). Ask for one now: `fctl review start -p my-app 12`. Reviews that run tests or start on a label: a GitHub Actions workflow with a run token ([Automation](https://fctl.sh/docs/automation.md)).
7. **Agents that fix their own pull requests**: `fctl projects set -p my-app --follow-ups all` (the default for new projects); then anyone who can write to the repository comments `@fctl please split this function` on the pull request, and failed checks and conflicts come back to the agent on their own. Needs the instance's GitHub webhook.
8. **Linear**: a workspace admin who is a Linear admin runs `fctl workspaces linear connect`; a maintainer picks the teams (`fctl projects set -p my-app --tickets linear --linear-team ENG`, or `ENG,DES` for several, the first where agents file new tickets; optionally `--linear-project "Mobile app"`, or `DES:Website` to name the team); each person links their Linear account once (`fctl account linear connect`). Then assigning an issue to fctl (it becomes the delegate) or mentioning fctl starts a session as that person, names the branch after the issue key, and posts the agent's steps, pull requests and replies in the issue; replies there reach the agent. fctl moves the issue to In Progress as a delegated issue's session starts (a mention's once its agent changes something), to In Review when a turn ends with the session's pull request up, and to Done once its pull requests merged, one that says `Fixes ENG-123` among them; `--linear-start`, `--linear-review` and `--linear-done` (`on`/`off`) choose which moves fctl makes. The `explore` label asks for a plan first.
9. **GitHub Issues as the tracker**: the default; agents use `gh issue` in the repositories they write to. `fctl projects set -p my-app --tickets github --tickets-repo owner/name` keeps them to one repository's issues (through `fctl ticket` when they write to other repositories too); `--tickets none` keeps them away from trackers. A maintainer can start a session that reaches GitHub's issues whatever the tracker says, to move them into Linear, say (`fctl run --github-issues`).
10. **Plan or review without changes**: `fctl run -p my-app -d --github read "Plan the move to Postgres: what changes, in what order, what can break."` or a project-wide cap: `fctl projects set -p my-app --github comment`.
11. **Set up a project** (a workspace admin): `fctl projects create "My app" --repo my-org/my-app -w acme`, then `fctl projects set -p my-app --setup-script 'npm ci' --idle-timeout 30 --pr-descriptions balanced`, more repositories with `fctl projects repos add my-org/my-lib --write -p my-app`, an image with `--image ghcr.io/acme/agent:1` or `--build Dockerfile`, size with `--cpus 8 --memory 16g`, shared package caches with `--package-caches on`, its agents' instructions, model and effort with `--instructions-file agents.md --model opus --effort high`, the context size Claude compacts their sessions near with `--compact-window 400k` (100k to 1m; `default` for Claude's, near the model's whole window), opening pull requests when they finish with `--auto-pull-request on|off`, how they handle pull requests and issues with `--pr-instructions-file prs.md` (`fctl projects show my-app --pr-instructions` prints fctl's rules to start from), Remote Control and claude.ai connectors with `--remote-control on|off --connectors on|off`, its name, description and default branch with `--name "Web app" --description "The storefront" --default-branch develop`, and its icon in the sidebar and on its page with `--icon store --icon-color yellow --icon-style duotone` (an [IconMCP](https://iconmcp.com) glyph's name; ink, yellow, pink, blue or a color of its own as `'#rrggbb'`; outline, duotone or solid; `--icon ""` for the one that fits its name). Secrets: `fctl projects secrets set STRIPE_KEY -p my-app`, the value typed at its prompt or piped in; `fctl projects secrets -p my-app` lists their names. People: `fctl projects members add grace@example.com --role maintainer -p my-app` (`viewer`, `editor`, `maintainer`, `owner`), `fctl projects members role …`, `fctl projects members remove …`.
12. **Bring a machine online** (its owner, at its terminal): install Apple's `container` (macOS 26+, `container system start`; a host on the apple driver starts it again after the Mac restarts, stops a sandbox whose VM stops answering, which would hold up every other: its session fails and resumes in it, and restarts Apple's `container` when its sandboxes lose the network while the Mac has it, at most every 30 minutes: sessions wait meanwhile rather than fail), Lima, or Docker (on Linux, Docker Engine with `sudo systemctl enable --now docker`; `fctl host install` offers to add the user to the `docker` group, and fctl takes the group itself, with no new login), or on Linux with KVM `passt` and `e2fsprogs` for `--driver firecracker`; then `fctl login`, `fctl host install --workspace acme` (or `--token fctl_rt_…` from the workspace's Runners tab), `fctl host doctor`, `fctl host status`. Maintenance: `fctl host drain --wait` (`--timeout 60s` stops what still runs after that long, as a cloud takes the machine; give it a minute less than the notice), `fctl host undrain`; a machine that should go once idle: `fctl host install --retire-when-idle 20m --retire-command '…'`; an autopilot whose own session's sandbox is on a draining runner moves off at its next wake once its turn has ended, in a fresh session on another runner, as it does while the machine is away and another runner would run it, and `fctl host status` lists the autopilots that wake there, with when each wakes. Many machines, or ones autoscaling starts: a workspace admin makes an enrollment token (`fctl runners enrollment-tokens create "Build fleet" -w acme --max-runners 20 --remove-offline-after 5m`, `--approval` to approve each), or any member one for their own sessions (`--personal`), and each machine's boot script runs `FCTL_SERVER=https://app.fctl.sh FCTL_ENROLL_TOKEN=fctl_et_… fctl host install` with no sign-in (and, for someone who keeps their Claude token on their runners, `fctl host claude set-token < /run/secrets/claude-token`); `fctl runners --pending`, `fctl runners approve <runner>`, `fctl runners reject <runner>`, `fctl runners remove <runner>`. Pools: `--labels aws,large` on the token, `fctl runners enrollment-tokens set "AWS large" -w acme --placement packed --max-runners 40`, `fctl projects set -p ml --runners large` (in the web app: Pools on the Runners tab, and a pool by its name in a project's Settings → Runners); an autoscaler reads `GET /api/v1/runner/enroll/demand` with the enrollment token (KEDA: `valueLocation: wanted`), or `fctl runners demand -w acme --pool "AWS large" --json`.
13. **Dashboards and reports**: a token with `--access read` lists sessions, transcripts, memory and retrospectives and starts nothing: `fctl sessions --active --json`, `fctl sessions --since 1d --json` (at work in the last day, those that ended in it too), `fctl pulls --json` (the open pull requests agents opened, each once with the sessions that list it; `-p my-app`, `--state merged|closed|all`, `--mine`; archived sessions' too, a session marked `(asks you)` or `(archived)`, `archived` and `question` in its JSON; the app's `/pulls` page sorts the open ones by what each needs next: waiting for your answer, ready for review, checks failing, agents at work, merge queue, drafts), `fctl retro list -p my-app --json`, `fctl search "flaky test" --json`, `fctl logs my-app#12 --json`, `fctl diff my-app#12` (the branch's changes as git prints them; `--json` for each file's patch).
14. **Keep agents informed**: `fctl memory add -p my-app "Deploys happen on Thursdays: merge migrations by Tuesday."`; delete every stale note at once with `fctl memory delete --stale -p my-app` (a project keeps 1,000 notes, stale ones included), or have fctl delete notes once they have been stale a number of days with `fctl projects set -p my-app --stale-note-days 7` (1 to 365; `never` by default); read what they learned with `fctl memory -p my-app` and `fctl retro list -p my-app --outcome blocked`.
15. **Hand a session to someone** (its owners): `fctl share <session> grace@example.com` lets someone in its workspace view it and message its agent (`--role viewer` only views it, `--role owner` also stops, resumes, archives and shares it), `fctl share <session>` lists who it is shared with, `fctl unshare <session> grace@example.com` takes it back. Anyone who can message the agent can have it hand over the sandbox's secrets and tokens. `fctl archive <session>` takes a finished session out of the lists and stops follow-ups reaching it (`fctl unarchive`, `fctl sessions --archived`).

## Web app

- **Agent Floor** (`/`): the task box (project, model, effort, GitHub access, files; ⌘Enter starts, **Schedule** turns the task into a schedule), sessions **Working now** and **Recently** (choosing one of your workspaces above them lists only its sessions and moves the task box to its first project where you can start sessions, in your sidebar order), plan usage, invitations. ⌘K searches sessions, projects, workspaces and what sessions said.
- **Keyboard shortcuts** (on a computer; ⌘ is Ctrl on Linux and Windows): `?` or ⌘/ lists them all, those of the page first, with a filter (also in ⌘K and the menu under your name); `n`, or ⌘⇧O from a text box, opens the Agent Floor's task box over any page, with the same draft, in the page's project (on the Agent Floor or a project's Sessions tab, it goes to the page's own box); `g` then `f`, `n`, `p` or `s` go to the Agent Floor, the next session in Needs you, the pull requests and Settings; ⌘K, ⌘B (fold the sidebar); on a session's page `r` goes to the message box, `c` opens the changes, `d` shows or hides the details, and `j`/`k` go from turn to turn. Esc leaves a task box or the message box, for the single keys. Keys are the characters your layout types: `?` and `/` work with the Shift they take on Swedish or German keyboards, letters where each layout has them.
- **Sidebar**: the Agent Floor; **Needs you** (what your sessions and those you follow wait on you for, most pressing first: an agent's question, a failure, failed checks, a pull request its agent finished, a reply it waits for unless its pull requests are all merged or closed and nobody wrote to it since, a pause; its count shows in the tab's title and on the installed app's icon); **Pull requests** (`/pulls`, with how many are ready for review); then your workspaces and their projects in your order, each project with its icon, and under each, on every page, its autopilot while it is on or paused (an Autopilot line that opens the autopilot's own session, with its comet running while it works, when it wakes next, Paused, or in blue how many things it asks you, which opens its Autopilot tab), then its sessions that haven't ended and, for an hour, those that stopped or failed; hovering one whose agent waits for a message, stopped or failed shows a button that hides it from the sidebar in that browser until its agent works again (a run starts, it asks something or it ends another turn). The project a page is about shows its own pull requests too. Drag its edge to make it wider (a double click puts it back); ⌘B (Ctrl+B; ⌘\ too), or dragging its edge most of the way to the left, folds it into a rail of icons, and dragging the rail's edge to the right opens it again.
- **Pull requests** (`/pulls`): the pull requests agents opened, each once with its sessions, archived sessions' too; open ones sorted by what each needs next (waiting for your answer, with the agent's question and its answers to click, then ready for review, checks failing, agents at work, merge queue, drafts), merged and closed ones by day; each with its checks, fctl's review and its size; a filter whose matches each tab counts, a workspace or project, Mine (on until you turn it off, which the browser keeps; the sidebar's counts follow it); opened again from the sidebar, it shows the tab and the filter it had; `j`/`k`, Enter, `o` for GitHub, `c` to copy its link, `/` to filter, the arrows between tabs.
- **Session page** (`/s/<id>`, `r`, `c` and `d` for the message box, the changes and the details, `j`/`k` from turn to turn): the live transcript (tool calls fold into lines, edits show highlighted; the images the agent read show small under them for 7 days), the composer to message the agent (with its owner's lists for the model and effort level it works at from its next step: a new model, which reads the conversation again without Claude's prompt cache, asks first), Interrupt, Stop and Resume, Share, the follow bell, Changes (the files the branch changed; a file opens every file's diff, highlighted, one after the other at that file, with the list of files beside them marking the one in view: `j`/`k` or the arrow keys in the list go from file to file, `n`/`p` from change to change, ⌘F finds in all the diffs (Enter and Shift+Enter, ⌘G, Alt+C/W/R for case, whole words and regular expressions), `s` lays them out side by side, `w` wraps lines; as the agent changes the files, its changes come in where the reader looks while the lines in view stay put, and a button goes to those out of sight), pull requests with checks, context and usage, retrospectives (the transcript shows each with a line for each part, which opens to all it says, and marks what an update changed), ⌘F to find in the transcript, Open in Claude. The page reads the session in turns: a cover with the session at a glance (turns, the agent's time, steps, changes, pull requests, a ribbon of the turns), then each message opens a card, the agent's work hangs from it on a thread, and each turn ends with its time, steps and the files it edited (each opens its diff), and copies as Markdown or a link to it (`/s/<id>?turn=<seq>`); the agent's plan (its TodoWrite list) stays in the details; a line above the message box says what the agent does now and where it is in its plan, or that it's the reader's turn, and while the agent waits for its background tasks, names them in a list that goes to the call that started each (whose line says it runs in the background, then how long it ran); a bar under the header says which turn the reader is in and lists them all (the details list the newest six and the one the reader is in, the earlier ones a click away), a button goes back to the newest work or up to what came while the reader was away, and the conversation alone shows without the agent's work.
- **Project page** (`/p/<slug>`): Sessions, Autopilot (where the workspace lets projects have one: putting the project on autopilot, then where it stands, what it asks you, notes to steer it, its direction, plan, files, sessions and log), Schedules, Reviews, Memory (its notes, `?tab=memory`, and its retrospectives, `?tab=retrospectives`), Repositories, Members and Settings tabs. Settings is a page each, `?tab=`: General (`general`: name, description, icon, default branch, deleting it), Agents (`agents`: instructions, model and effort, the context size Claude compacts near, access on GitHub and to claude.ai, memory and retrospectives), Pull requests (`pull-requests`: opening them, commit credits, screenshots, follow-ups), Tickets (`tickets`), Sandbox (`sandbox`: setup script, caches, image, size, idle timeout, environment) and Secrets (`secrets`); owners and maintainers see and change them all, and everyone else in the project reads Tickets there. Each page saves on its own. Without a page, a phone lists them and a wider screen opens General beside them.
- **Workspace page** (`/w/<slug>`): Projects, People, Runners (with the command and token that add one, its pools with what each needs now and their runners, a new pool made step by step with what its cloud needs and every value filled in, the runners that wait for your approval, and the enrollment tokens: every one for admins, members' own for members), GitHub, Linear, Settings (its name, address, avatar image, and the color its avatar shows without one: yellow, pink, blue, ink or one of its own, as `fctl workspaces set --color '#2a9d8f'` sets it), and the Audit log for admins.
- **Settings** (`/settings`, a page each, `?tab=`): Profile (`profile`: name and picture; without one, your Gravatar unless you turn it off), Email addresses (`emails`, with commit emails), Workspaces (`workspaces`: which Claude connection, leaving), Claude (`claude`), Linear (`linear`, your Linear account), Notifications (`notifications`), Appearance (`appearance`: dark or light, a 12- or 24-hour clock), App log (`log`: what the app did in this browser lately, kept only there, to copy into a report), Security (`security`: password and Google, passkeys, two-factor sign-in, devices), Access tokens (`tokens`) and Your data (`data`: one export a week, unless admins chose another wait, and deleting your account). Without `?tab=`, a phone lists the pages and a wider screen opens Profile beside them. **Admin** (`/admin`, instance admins): people, access (allowlist), sign-in (`?tab=sign-in`: how people sign in, the providers with their redirect URIs, the domains that require one, whether signing in makes accounts, two-factor sign-in), early access, workspaces, GitHub, runners, settings (with reserved addresses, Gravatar for everyone, how often people can export their data, and admin tokens where the instance takes them), audit.
- Notifications are Web Push to browsers where people turned them on (on iPhone and iPad, fctl added to the Home Screen): a followed session waits for a reply, pauses on a usage limit, or fails; an autopilot's own session, and those it starts while it is on, only when they ask something, or when the autopilot's own sessions failed four times in a row, and each day they go on failing (fctl doesn't pause it for failures: it tries again 5, 15 and 60 minutes later, then every hour until one works).

## Docs

- [Overview](https://fctl.sh/docs/index.md): the three pieces (control plane, runners, clients), where to go next, and the words the docs use.
- [Getting started](https://fctl.sh/docs/getting-started.md): signing in, installing the CLI, workspaces, connecting Claude, bringing a machine online, creating a project, starting, following and steering sessions, working together, roles.
- [The CLI](https://fctl.sh/docs/cli.md): every command: sign-in and access tokens, sessions and sharing them, search, workspaces, projects with their secrets and members, repositories, ticket trackers, memory and retrospectives, review agents, schedules, notifications, Claude, hosts and `host.toml`, admin, your account, updating, exit codes.
- [fctl for agents](https://fctl.sh/docs/agents.md): driving fctl from agents, scripts and other programs: tokens, what a personal agent asks its person before it signs in, waiting for sessions, reading transcripts, JSON and exit codes, pitfalls, recipes in full, and what agents do inside a session's sandbox.
- [The HTTP API](https://fctl.sh/docs/api.md): authentication, errors, paging, and the endpoints for sessions, messages, events, schedules, projects, memory, retrospectives and reviews, with examples.
- [Automation](https://fctl.sh/docs/automation.md): schedules, schedules that run on events on GitHub, Linear delegation, starting agents from other tools, access tokens, GitHub access levels, review agents from GitHub Actions, other uses.
- [Self-hosting](https://fctl.sh/docs/self-hosting.md): the control plane in a container (Docker, Kubernetes) or on Cloudflare, settings, HTTPS, a private instance with only the paths GitHub, Linear and the clouds call open to the internet, the first account, provisioning people with admin tokens, the GitHub App (each field of its form, permissions, webhook events, follow-ups), the optional review app, the Linear app (its form and webhook events), Google sign-in, email, hosts.
- [Identity tokens](https://fctl.sh/docs/identity-tokens.md): OIDC tokens with which agents prove to your services and clouds that a request comes from one of your sessions: `fctl id-token`, every claim and the subject, checking a token (jose, PyJWT), AWS roles with trust policies and session tags, Google Cloud workload identity, Azure federated credentials, secrets for the setup script from the clouds' secret stores, Vault, what a token proves.
- [fctl for organizations](https://fctl.sh/docs/organizations.md): running fctl for a company: its own instance and the settings organizations change, provisioning people from a directory with admin tokens and letting in nobody else, service accounts for portals and bots that start sessions for people, access tokens and schedules for CI and other tools, webhooks to other tools with recipes, enrollment tokens for fleets of runners, audit logs, and every credential at a glance.
- [Runners in your cloud](https://fctl.sh/docs/runners-in-your-cloud.md): a guide to a fleet of runners on AWS, Google Cloud or Azure that grows and shrinks with the work: a machine image with Docker, fctl and the sandbox image, an enrollment token in the cloud's secret store, sizing a machine's sessions, hardening, draining each machine before the cloud removes it (EC2 lifecycle hooks, Compute Engine graceful shutdown, Azure terminate notifications), sizing the group to the sessions that wait for it (`fctl runners demand`, machines that size their group or retire themselves once idle), Spot machines; the files it builds on and reference deployments in Terraform (an AWS module with an EC2 Image Builder image and a sizer Lambda, smaller Google Cloud and Azure examples) are in the repository's `deploy/cloud`.
